messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: biglm and rstanarm optimization
parts:
Hi all. Phil was telling me how he's running simple regressions with big datasets and using the R package biglm which feeds the data into lm() piece by piece so R's memory won't choke. I was thinking maybe we should build something that would do the same thing for rstanarm. When stan_lm() or stan_glm() is in optimization mode, it's super-fast, so this would seem to make a lot of sense, no?
A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] biglm and rstanarm optimization
parts:
How big is big? Doing this with anything other than
stochastic gradient for really big problems is madness.
And by really big, I mean ones that won't fit into memory.

Then if you have sparse predictors, you really really need
sparse arithmetic.

Something like Vowpal Wabbit can scale pretty well for
these kinds of problems, though it's not exact given the way
it encodes features.

Just writing the linear model in Stan and optimizing will
be faster than lm() and more scalable probably. Don't know
how RStan impacts this equation, but in CmdStan you can
run medium-sized data sets (not what I'd call big and nothing
that won't fit in memory).

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] biglm and rstanarm optimization
parts:
On Friday, March 31, 2017 at 3:00:50 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
How big is big?

Pretty much unlimited in the number of observations. The stan_{big}lm() function uses OLS estimates as sufficient statistics to evaluate the likelihood and the biglm() function produces OLS estimates by incrementally updating the QR decomposition as each batch of data is read off the disk. Both the biglm part and the Stan part of stan_biglm() are quadratic in the number of predictors.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] biglm and rstanarm optimization
parts:
On Friday, March 31, 2017 at 3:48:49 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Neat.    I had no idea there were functions like that in
RStanArm.  Is there a feature list somewhere?
There is a list of the stan_foo fitting functions in the overview page of the doc, but we don't re-document what foo() does.

They're quadratic rather than cubic?  I thought you needed
to solve N x N matrices where there are N predictors?

The biglm() function is documented to be quadratic in the number of predictors for memory. It does a bunch of Jacobi rotations, which is presumably of cubic complexity, but that only has to be done once. After it gets to Stan, the log-likelihood is pretty much just a dot_self() on the difference between the OLS coefficients and the proposed coefficients (in orthogonalized coordinates, so it is Euclidean distance rather than Mahalanobis).

I guess that's all feasible with the simple structure of LMs.
For GLMs, I've always seen stochastic gradient used.  Would there
be a way to do something similar under the link function for
logistic regression?

No.

Ben
